{{short description|Singaporean chemist and writer}}
'''Li Lienfung''' (1923 – 3 August 2011) 李廉凤 was a [[Singaporeans|Singaporean]] chemist and writer. She was a bilingual writer, using both [[English language|English]] and [[Chinese language|Chinese]]. Li was known for her plays, short stories and especially for her newspaper column, "Bamboo Green."

== Biography ==
Li was born in [[Shanghai]] in 1923.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_1829_2011-08-18.html|title=Li Lienfung|last=Chua|first=Alivin|website=Infopedia Singapore|publisher=National Library Board Singapore|access-date=2017-11-28}}</ref> Her father, Li Kuo Ching, left to work in the [[United States]], leaving Li's mother to raise her in [[China]].<ref name=":4" /> He eventually abandoned his family when Li's mother would not move to the U.S.<ref name=":3" /> When China was invaded by [[Japan]] in 1937, she moved to [[Hunan]], and then to [[Hong Kong]].<ref name=":3" />

She went to [[Mills College]] in 1940 and graduated with a degree in [[chemistry]].<ref name=":3" /> She worked for a short time in an [[Aluminium smelting|aluminum smelting]] plant in New Jersey as a lab assistant.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Stevenson|first=Sarah|date=31 March 2011|title=Around the World in 80 Years|url=https://issuu.com/millsquarterly/docs/2011spring/14|journal=Mills Quarterly|volume=99|issue=3|pages=14–15|via=Issuu}}</ref> She studied [[organic chemistry]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), but transferred to [[Cornell University]] where she earned her master's degree in literature in 1946.<ref name=":5" /> At Cornell, her master's thesis was on [[Chinese literature|Chinese folk literature]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite news|url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19800308-1.2.138.3|title=The woman behind 'The Sword'|last=Mahbubani|first=Gretchen|date=8 March 1980|work=The Straits Times|access-date=2017-11-29}}</ref>

In July 1946, she married Ho Rih Hwa, who was also a student at Cornell.<ref name=":3" /> She and her father also reconciled at this time.<ref name=":3" /> Her father sent her to [[Bangkok]] in 1948, where she became the chief chemist analyzing [[tungsten ore]]s that her father exported, trading with the [[Wah Chang Corporation|Wah Chang]] Group company.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":3" /> Her family then moved to [[Yangon]] in 1949.<ref name=":3" /> Later, Li helped her father set up tapioca factories and other food-related ventures.<ref name=":5" />

Li's daughter, [[Minfong Ho|Ho Minfong]], was born in Yangon in 1951.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v9QEBAAAQBAJ&q=%22li+lienfung%22&pg=PA340|title=Southeast Asian Personalities of Chinese Descent: A Biographical Dictionary, Volume I & II|last=Koh|first=Tai Ann|date=2012|publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies|isbn=9789814345217|editor-last=Suryadinata|editor-first=Leo|pages=340|language=en|chapter=Ho Minfong}}</ref> Minfong would go on to become a noted writer.<ref name=":2" /> Her son, [[Ho Kwon Ping]], was born in [[Hong Kong]] in 1952 and later became a businessman.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v9QEBAAAQBAJ&q=%22li+lienfung%22&pg=PA336|title=Southeast Asian Personalities of Chinese Descent: A Biographical Dictionary, Volume I & II|last=Tan|first=Kevin Y.L.|date=2012|publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies|isbn=9789814345217|editor-last=Suryadinata|editor-first=Leo|pages=336|language=en|chapter=Ho Kwon Ping}}</ref> Li has another son, Kwon Cjan, who is also involved in business.<ref name=":5" /> In 1952, Li returned to work for the company, and was eventually made the vice-chair of Wah Chang.<ref name=":3" />

Li's husband became Singapore's ambassador to [[Thailand]] in 1967.<ref name=":5" /> After Thailand, he was made the ambassador to several [[Europe]]an countries and entities, meaning that Li lived in Europe until the early 1970s, when they moved to Singapore.<ref name=":5" />

Li died on 3 August 2011 after going into a [[coma]] following a massive [[Intracerebral hemorrhage|brain haemorrhage]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Lim |first=David |date=5 August 2011 |title=Bilingual writer Li Lienfung dies at 88 |url=http://www.asiaone.com/News/AsiaOne+News/Singapore/Story/A1Story20110805-292784.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201034839/http://www.asiaone.com/News/AsiaOne+News/Singapore/Story/A1Story20110805-292784.html |archive-date=2017-12-01 |access-date=2024-04-01 }}</ref> She died in the [[National University Hospital]].<ref name=":3" /> Li was inducted into the [[Singapore Women's Hall of Fame]] in 2014.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Li Lienfung|url=https://www.swhf.sg/profiles/li-lienfung/|access-date=2021-08-11|website=Singapore Women's Hall of Fame|language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Work ==
''The Sword Has Two Edges'' had its origins in research she started in 1956 on the story of ''[[Romance of the Three Kingdoms|San Guo Shi Yan Yi]]''.<ref name=":6" /> Li wrote the manuscript quickly and when she was asked to rewrite it as a comedy, she put it away, only to revisit the story in 1971.<ref name=":6" /> A member of the Experimental Theatre Group, D. Murugan, decided to produce the play in 1977.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.straitstimes.com/lifestyle/entertainment/one-of-singapores-first-english-political-plays-are-you-there-singapore|title=One of Singapore's first English political plays, Are You There, Singapore?, might never have seen light of day|last=Tan|first=Corrie|date=2014-07-22|work=The Straits Times|access-date=2017-11-29|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":6" /> Her next play, ''Trials and Turbulence of the Twilight Years'' won a first place award in its category from the [[Ministry of Communications and Information|Ministry of Culture]] in 1978.<ref name=":3" /> In 1981, her play, ''The Late Storm'' was produced.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19811217-1.2.188.2|title=Play highlights problems of aged in modern society|last=Fan|first=Yi Fu|date=17 December 1981|work=The Straits Times|access-date=2017-11-29}}</ref>

Li wrote a popular column in English and Chinese, called "Bamboo Green" which ran between 1979 and 1984 in ''[[The Straits Times]]''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=http://www.purduesports.com/sports/w-baskbl/spec-rel/042612aaa.html|title=Li's Personal Glimpses|last=Lee|first=San Chouy|date=26 July 1993|work=The Straits Times|access-date=28 November 2017|url-access=subscription|via=LexisNexis|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201042219/http://www.purduesports.com/sports/w-baskbl/spec-rel/042612aaa.html|archive-date=1 December 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1986, a compilation of her columns, ''A Joss Stick for My Mother'' was released.<ref name=":4" /> Li revived the column in 1993, and continued to write it until 1998.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> The column educated Singaporeans on Chinese history, literature, life and culture.<ref name=":0" /> Li then started writing a Chinese column for the ''[[Lianhe Zaobao]]'' between 1998 and 2009.<ref name=":1" />

Li published the Chinese version of her [[memoir]], ''A Daughter Remembers'', in 2010, with the English translation coming out after her death.<ref name=":4" />
